system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- Evidence text comes from a PDF text layer. If symbols are garbled so that you cannot verify the atom, answer "hold" for that check and say so.
- Be strict. When unsure between pass and a non-pass value, choose the non-pass value and explain.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom. pass = fully stated. revise = the core claim is stated, and the gap is only wording, strength, or a dropped/extra peripheral qualifier that can be fixed by deleting or softening words (say what). fail = not stated, OR the atom adds substantive content the evidence lacks: a scope or population restriction (e.g. 'In B-ALL'), a mechanism or operation, a characterization (e.g. 'an unbounded while loop'), or a formula/definition. If deleting the unsupported part would change what the atom tests, it is fail, not revise. For pass, put the supporting evidence ids in cite (required).
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / revise / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge: one fact a person who studied the concept would simply know. revise = the core fact is recall-level but the sentence carries extra load that must be removed, e.g. stacked conditions (since/although/if ... and ...), a procedural or evaluative add-on ('easy to define but requires checking ...'), or a clause that introduces a second technical concept that must be known separately (e.g. 'if X is an inner Kan complex' when that is not the card concept). fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = the authors' opinion or choice, or the finding of one study, so the answer is not fixed without the source.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a single system, product, or one study's topic.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}
user:
CONCEPT: Data dependences
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Covers RAW, WAR and WAW dependences (and RAR as non-constraining) as expressed through accessors in the task graph DAG, and what they imply for ordering and data movement. Excludes event-based and in-order queue mechanisms except as contrast.

ATOMS:
- DPCPP2-C04-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: A Read-after-Write (RAW) dependence occurs when one task needs to read data produced by a different task, and it describes the flow of data between the two kernels.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0230-s08] The first, Read-after-Write (RAW), occurs when one task needs to read data produced by a different task.
    [DPCPP2-p0230-s09] This type of dependence describes the flow of data between two kernels.
- DPCPP2-C04-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: A Write-after-Read (WAR) dependence occurs when one task needs to update data after another task has read it, and it is also called an anti-dependence.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0230-s10] The second type of dependence happens when one task needs to update data after another task has read it.
    [DPCPP2-p0230-s11] We call that type of dependence a Write-after-Read (WAR) dependence.
    [DPCPP2-p0121-s04] WAR dependences are also called anti-dependences.
- DPCPP2-C04-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: A Write-after-Write (WAW) dependence occurs when two tasks try to write the same data, and it is also called an output dependence.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0230-s12] The final type of data dependence occurs when two tasks try to write the same data.
    [DPCPP2-p0230-s13] This is known as a Write-after-Write (WAW) dependence.
    [DPCPP2-p0121-s10] The WAW dependence, also called an output dependence, ensures that the final output will be correct on the host.
- DPCPP2-C04-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: In a task graph, which is a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are tasks and whose edges are dependences, the edges are one-way because a dependence means task A must happen before task B.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0111-s07] This task graph is specifically a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where the nodes are the tasks and the edges are the dependences.
    [DPCPP2-p0111-s08] The graph is directed because dependences are one-way: task A must happen before task B.
    [DPCPP2-p0111-s09] The graph is acyclic because it cannot contain any cycles or paths from a node that lead back to itself.
- DPCPP2-C04-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: A RAW dependence between a kernel and the host, arising because the host wants to read a buffer after the kernel has finished, forces the runtime to copy that buffer back to the host.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0119-s05] Finally, we also create a RAW dependence on buffer c_buf between kernel computeC and the host since the host wants to read C after the kernel has finished.
    [DPCPP2-p0119-s06] This forces the runtime to copy buffer c_buf back to the host.
- DPCPP2-C04-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: RAW dependences ensure that data flows in the correct direction between computations, while WAR dependences ensure that existing values are not overwritten before they are read.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0121-s05] RAW dependences ensure that data properly flows in the correct direction, while WAR dependences ensure existing values are not overwritten before they are read.
- DPCPP2-C04-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: A Read-after-Read (RAR) scenario, where two kernels only read the same buffer through read-only accessors, places no extra restrictions on the runtime, so the kernels are free to execute in any order, including at the same time.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0118-s04] kernel readA is submitted after kernel computeB, this creates a Read-after-Read (RAR) scenario.
    [DPCPP2-p0118-s05] However, RARs do not place extra restrictions on the runtime, and the kernels are free to execute in any order.
    [DPCPP2-p0118-s06] Indeed, a runtime might prefer to execute kernel readA before kernel computeB or even execute both at the same time.
- DPCPP2-C04-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: Even if a kernel only writes to a buffer, the buffer's original content may still be moved to the device, because there is no guarantee that the kernel will write all values in the buffer.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0119-s01] even if a kernel will only write to a buffer, the original content of the buffer may still be moved to the device because there is no guarantee that all values in the buffer will be written by a kernel (see Chapter 7 for tags that let us optimize in these cases).
- DPCPP2-C04-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: SYCL graphs ensure correct execution only based on the dependences that have been expressed, so the programmer is responsible for making sure the graph correctly expresses all dependences in the program.
  EVIDENCE:
    [DPCPP2-p0230-s16] No matter which types of graph a computation needs, SYCL graphs ensure that a program will execute correctly based on the expressed dependences.
    [DPCPP2-p0230-s17] However, it is up to the programmer to make sure that a graph correctly expresses all the dependences in a program.
